THE BOARD
What's actually going on.
Tuesday, November 17, 2026Priced, Not Settled
What’s Moved Verdict Shenzhen Bridges The Fed Houston Texas Two Rival Reads Scenarios Watchlist

The Board

Everyone moved this week. Nothing was decided.

A bridge span fell in the Kerch Strait, three presidents prepared to sit down in Shenzhen, a Federal Reserve hike got priced as a certainty, and Texas started arguing over who holds power in January. Every visible move was cheap and reversible. The veto holders have not moved at all.

By Josh Pilcher
Scroll

The Kerch Strait

The arch is down. The trains are running.

Ukraine says it dropped a span of the bridge that supplies Crimea. Russia has repaired this crossing three times. The fourth repair is the week’s real story.

Photograph by Rosavtodor, via Wikimedia Commons. The Kerch Bridge in 2019, before this week’s strikes. Kyiv says a road arch and span fell on the night of November 16 and 17, 2026; rail traffic resumed on Tuesday.

What’s Moved

Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge for a second straight night. Kyiv says a road arch and span fell into the strait. Rail traffic, the military bulk carrier, resumed on Tuesday after a brief pause. Russia hit Kyiv’s bridges over the Dnipro the same night.

The EU Council approved a payment of just under 8 billion euros to Ukraine on November 16, the largest single payment under the Ukraine Facility. The Commission paid out 1.71 billion euros the same day for drones, ammunition and air defence.

All three capitals have confirmed a first meeting of the American, Chinese and Russian presidents, in Shenzhen on November 19. Washington says Ukraine is not on that agenda and no agreement is expected.

The Quad leaders met in Manila on November 17 for the first time in more than two years, 48 hours before the Shenzhen meeting they are meant to balance.

Futures markets put roughly 95 percent on a quarter-point Federal Reserve hike on December 9. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said on November 17 that several hikes are likely needed by spring. The 10-year Treasury closed at 5.15 percent on November 13.

Outgoing Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick backed changing Senate rules to strip powers from his Democratic successor before she takes the gavel. Houston’s Senfronia Thompson says she has 90 pledges for Speaker of the House, 14 more than she needs.

ERCOT’s chief executive asked the coming Texas Legislature for power to cut data centers before a grid emergency, not during one.

Verdict

Nothing was settled this week. Everything was priced.

A bridge strike, a summit photograph, a futures print and an executive order are all cheap moves. Each costs the actor little, can be walked back, and exists mainly to change the price of a negotiation that has not happened yet.

The decisions that would actually settle something are all still ahead. The three presidents meet on Thursday with no agreement expected and the largest war in Europe kept off their agenda. Europe’s money for Ukraine in 2027 is being fought over now and decided later. The Federal Reserve votes on December 9, one day before the November inflation data that might have changed its mind. Texas does not change hands until January 19, a week after its Legislature convenes and starts writing the rules the new officeholders will govern under.

Watch the veto holders, not the performers. A Republican Texas Senate, reluctant European governments and a railway timetable in Crimea have moved less this week than everyone else. They are the board.

[SCENE]

Shenzhen has closed its roads for the week.

Cars with plates from outside the city are banned from most districts. Drones are grounded. More than 1.5 million car owners have pledged to stay off the roads, in exchange for stickers and transit cards.

The city is being cleared for the 33rd APEC leaders’ meeting, which opens on Wednesday. Twenty-one economies. Xi Jinping in the chair.

On Thursday, if the schedules hold, Xi will sit down with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. It would be the first time the sitting presidents of the United States, China and Russia have met in one room.

Shenzhen is the argument before anyone speaks. In 1980 it was a border town of roughly 30,000 people, chosen as one of China’s first special economic zones, the place where market reform would be allowed to prove itself. China hosted APEC in Shanghai in 2001 to join a system built by others, and in Beijing in 2014 to propose one. Shenzhen is neither. The host is not asking to join anything. The city itself is the exhibit, and its trade with the other APEC economies reached 3.23 trillion yuan, about $484 billion, in the first nine months of this year, up 40 percent and close to 70 percent of the city’s total, according to Shenzhen Customs.

Chapter One

Shenzhen

Three presidents, one room, no text. The meeting is the prize, and everyone at it has already been paid.

Start with what the trilateral is not.

It is not a negotiation with a text. No draft, format or readout mechanism has been published. A senior American official, lowering expectations in advance, said the United States does not expect to reach any kind of agreement. The meeting is intended, in that official’s words, as the beginning of a conversation.

It is not about Ukraine. The same official said Trump is not expected to raise the war with Xi and Putin, and no separate meeting between Trump and Putin is scheduled. The Ukraine file runs through a different room, in Berlin.

What is on the stated agenda is nuclear weapons and Iran. The nuclear part has a date attached to it. New START, the last treaty capping American and Russian strategic arsenals, expired on February 5, 2026. There is now no treaty-bound limit on the two largest arsenals in the world.

Trump wants a new arrangement that includes China. China has answered that demand in public and in advance. Its position is that asking Beijing to join is neither fair, reasonable nor realistic, because its arsenal is far smaller. SIPRI’s count puts China at roughly 620 warheads, against about 5,042 for the United States and 5,420 for Russia.

So the central item on the agenda has been refused by one of the three parties before the meeting starts. That is not a failure of the meeting. It tells you what the meeting is for.

For Xi, the gain is the room. Both rivals travel to his city, in his summit week, on his sequencing. He sets the venue and the guest list, and hosting is leverage even when nothing is decided.

For Trump, the gain is a first-ever headline at no cost. Because Washington has already excused the meeting from Ukraine and from any agreement, no outcome on Thursday can be scored as a failure.

For Putin, the gain is the seat itself. The thing isolation was supposed to deny him, a place at a three-power table as an equal, is delivered before he concedes anything. The meeting is his payment, not his price.

Underneath the photograph, the trade truce tells the same story in contract form. On November 9 and 10, both sides extended their suspensions for two more months. China’s suspension of an extra 24 percent tariff on American goods now runs to January 10, 2027, with a 10 percent tariff still collected. Washington extended all 178 of its Section 301 tariff exclusions to January 9.

Two months. Not a settlement, an extension of the pause, set to expire just after the holidays. And one piece was never paused at all: the licensing requirement China imposed in April 2025 on seven medium and heavy rare earths, the chokepoint material in magnets, motors and weapons, still operates today, truce or no truce. Beijing extended everything except the lever that matters most.

The insurance policy in Manila

Washington knew how Shenzhen would look, so it bought insurance first.

On Tuesday, 48 hours before the trilateral, the Quad leaders met in Manila: Trump, India’s Narendra Modi, Japan’s Sanae Takaichi and Australia’s Anthony Albanese. It was the first Quad leaders’ meeting in more than two years, the first of Trump’s second term, and the first ever held in a country that is not a member. The Philippines, chairing ASEAN this year, hosted a balancing coalition aimed at China, in China’s near abroad, without joining it.

Manila is where this format keeps being born. The Quad first met there in 2007, on the sidelines of an ASEAN meeting, and was revived there in 2017 after a decade asleep. The rhyme is exact: same city, same sidelines, same purpose. What changed is the level. In 2007 and 2017 it was officials, meeting quietly. In 2026 it is presidents and prime ministers, meeting loudly, two days before the main event in Shenzhen.

The deliverables were modest and partly recycled. An inaugural Quad Business Leaders’ Forum, to meet in early 2027. Cooperation on maritime surveillance, undersea cables, cyber security and counterterrorism. A Super Intelligence Accelerator, with more than $85 million announced for wider access to trusted AI systems across the Indo-Pacific.

That $85 million was first announced at the Quad foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on October 31. No budget line or named critical minerals counterparty has been published behind it. A signal assembled from October’s deliverables is a photograph, not a bloc move, and everyone at the table knows the difference.

India is the tell. Modi framed the Quad as a constructive and trusted partnership, with the emphasis on supply chains, technology and disaster response. New Delhi is keeping its options open in every direction at once. It is in the Quad on Tuesday. It is not an APEC member, so it is not in Shenzhen on Thursday. It loses nothing either way.

That is the honest picture of the week in Asia. Two tables, set 48 hours apart, each designed so that nobody at either of them has to commit to anything.

Chapter Two

Bridges for Bridges

A span fell in the Kerch Strait and Europe got a seat at the table. Both moves are about who gets to bargain, and who pays.

The Kerch Bridge has been attacked before. The repair record is the context for everything claimed this week.

A truck bomb dropped road spans and set rail fuel wagons alight in October 2022. The road fully reopened in February 2023, the rail line that May. Naval drones damaged a road span in July 2023. The bridge was fully back by October. Underwater explosives against the submerged supports in June 2025 closed it for hours, not months.

Three attacks, three new methods, and each time Russia repaired the crossing and traffic returned. Anyone reading this week’s strike as a first is reading it wrong.

What Ukraine says is different this time is the target inside the target. Kyiv says the operation ran for weeks in seven stages, wearing down the air defences, radars and electronic warfare around the bridge first, and that on the night of November 16 and 17 the final strikes brought down a road arch and a span into the Kerch Strait.

The evidence supports part of that. Photographs geolocated by CNN appear to show a section of the road bridge in the water and the parallel rail bridge still standing. Ukraine’s General Staff says the roadway is out of action and the rail arch is damaged. Russia’s Transport Ministry suspended road and rail traffic for assessment and has not confirmed the extent of the damage. Two people were killed in Crimea in the overnight attacks, according to the Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov.

The evidence does not support the larger claim. Rail traffic resumed on Tuesday after a brief pause, according to Interfax reporting carried by Reuters and Bloomberg. Rail is the mode that carries military bulk. A fallen road span forces Crimea’s road logistics onto ferries and the longer land route and raises the cost of everything that moves. It does not sever Crimea.

The repair estimate circulating, a year or longer for a fallen structure of some 6,000 tonnes, is a Ukrainian assessment. No engineering survey has been published. This is the first attack to drop the arch itself, and the object damaged is categorically different from 2022 and 2023. Russia’s repair record says do not assume it stays down.

Russia’s drone tallies for the two nights, each presented as a record, are not independently verified, and the figures Moscow has given for overlapping windows do not agree with each other. They are a claimant’s counts, and they measure nothing a reader can use.

What can be used is the reciprocity, because both sides stated it. The same night, Russian strikes hit Kyiv’s North and South bridges over the Dnipro River, disrupting water, heating and metro service in the capital, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Zelenskyy framed the Kerch strike openly as retaliation, noting that Russia strikes Ukrainian infrastructure, including bridges, every day.

Bridge for bridge, 48 hours before Putin sits down in Shenzhen, is not a logistics campaign. It is a price being set. Kyiv’s core risk this week is being bargained over in a room it is not in. The strike is a demonstration, timed to the summit, that Ukraine keeps a veto by escalation over any bargain struck without it. The demonstration works even if the span is repaired by spring.

The format fight is the negotiation

The diplomatic architecture moved more than the front did, and it moved in two directions at once.

On November 10 and 11, American, Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi. Europeans were present in the city and took no part, with no contact with the Russian delegation.

On November 16, the format cracked open. France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland, plus the European Commission, the European Council and NATO, joined talks with Ukraine and the American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner online, in full, for the first time. The sides agreed to meet in Berlin, under the Coalition of the Willing, on security guarantees, reconstruction and the format of the next round. No date for Berlin has been announced.

On the same day, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia has not agreed to any of it. Moscow has not consented to expand the talks beyond the three delegations, he said, and no date is agreed for a next round with Russia.

Both statements are true, and together they are the story. Berlin is a coordination meeting of Ukraine and its funders, not a negotiation with Russia. Its purpose is to make the Coalition’s consent something Washington and Moscow have to reckon with before they set a format without Europe, which Abu Dhabi showed they are willing to do.

Russia’s leverage here is refusal. It costs Moscow nothing to keep Europe outside the room, and every week Europe stays outside, the guarantees Europe would have to underwrite get negotiated by people who will not pay for them.

Germany is trying to change that price from the other side. In Brussels on November 17, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius announced $300 million from Germany toward a joint package with Norway to buy American Patriot missiles for Ukraine, focused on PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors. It is Germany’s fifth package under the PURL programme, the arrangement where Europeans pay and American factories supply. The mechanism matters more than the amount. Europe is buying its relevance in the negotiation with the only currency Washington accepts, orders for American weapons.

At NATO headquarters the same day, the Ukraine Defense Contact Group met with the Pentagon’s policy chief, Elbridge Colby, who is expected to present Washington’s review of American troop levels in Europe within weeks. That review is the other half of the linkage. Europe is paying for missiles while waiting to hear how many American soldiers stay.

Europe’s money, in three different states

Europe’s financing of Ukraine is real, large and routinely misdescribed, because three different pots of money sit at three different stages and get reported as one.

The first pot is approved. On November 16 the EU Council approved a payment of just under 8 billion euros under the Ukraine Facility, the largest single payment in the programme’s history. About 5 billion euros of it comes from the Ukraine Support Loan. Kyiv qualified by completing more than 20 reform steps, in justice, anti-corruption work, state asset management and energy. Approval is not transfer. The money will arrive soon, and once it does, Facility payments since mid-2024 pass 40 billion euros.

The second pot is paid. The same day, the Commission disbursed 1.71 billion euros under the defence side of the Support Loan, for drones, ammunition, air defence and radars. That loan, agreed in December 2025, is 90 billion euros for 2026 and 2027, split roughly 60 billion for defence and 30 billion for budget support, borrowed by the EU on the markets and repayable by Ukraine only if Russia pays reparations.

The third pot is locked, and unlocking it is easy. About 45 billion euros of that 90 billion is the 2027 half. A Commission proposal from October 30 would release it, 31.7 billion for defence industry and 13.3 billion for budget support. The three countries that opted out of the loan, Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia, cannot veto that release, because the loan was built under enhanced cooperation among the other 24 member states.

The fight is over a fourth pot that does not exist yet. An EU assessment puts Ukraine’s 2027 gap at 70 billion euros. The Commission is expected to propose a new loan of 45 billion euros, on top of the existing 90 billion, to cover about two thirds of that gap. That proposal needs a unanimous change to the EU’s financial rules, though a state can opt out without blocking the others. The binding fight is the 2028 to 2034 budget behind it, which does require every member state.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has told the Council president that Germany’s support for that budget depends on every member state committing to finance Ukraine from 2027. Slovakia’s Robert Fico called that blackmail and threatened a veto of the budget. European leaders take the fight up at their next summit.

The rate channel connects this to the next section. The EU borrows this money on markets priced off a world where the American 10-year yields more than 5 percent. Every point on that yield is a point on the cost of European solidarity. The Federal Reserve does not vote on Ukraine. It prices it.

Chapter Three

A Hike Priced Before It Is Voted

The December meeting is three weeks away. Futures have already held it, and the argument now is over the path, not the vote.

The Federal Reserve’s December meeting is three weeks away. The market has already held it.

Futures pricing on November 16 and 17 put roughly 95 percent on a quarter-point hike on December 9, with most of the remainder on a half point. Prediction markets sat a few points lower, around 90 to 93 percent for the quarter point. The venues disagree because they are built differently, futures splitting an implied rate between two outcomes and prediction markets pricing a hold explicitly. Anyone quoting a single figure as the odds is quoting a snapshot, not a fact. What the range says, consistently, is that a hold has been priced out.

The data behind the pricing is not in dispute. October inflation, published November 10, rose 0.4 percent on the month, with core prices up 0.3 percent for the third straight month. Three months at that pace annualises to about 3.6 percent, well above the 2 percent target. Payrolls rose by 165,000 in October and unemployment fell to 4.1 percent. The economy grew at a 3.4 percent annual rate in the third quarter, and spending by private domestic buyers rose 4.9 percent.

One gap in the data deserves a single mention. The Bureau of Labor Statistics published no 12-month inflation rate for October, because October 2025 prices were never collected during last year’s shutdown. The Fed is steering by monthly momentum because the annual gauge has a hole in it.

The committee’s own voices have split by speed, not direction.

Governor Christopher Waller said on November 10 that he supports a quarter-point hike in December, and that a half point should be considered if core inflation came in at 0.3 percent or higher. It came in at exactly 0.3 percent.

Dallas President Lorie Logan wants at least two more quarter-point hikes before any pause.

St. Louis President Alberto Musalem went furthest, on November 17. Several rate increases will likely be needed before the spring of 2027, he said. His measure is the real rate, the policy rate after inflation: he argued it needs to reach 2 to 2.5 percent by spring, from roughly 1 to 1.5 percent now.

The tightening is already real, and it is in the long end. The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.15 percent on November 13 and at 5.12 percent on November 16. On November 13 the real yield, after inflation, stood at 2.91 percent, while the market’s long-term inflation expectation sat near 2.24 percent. Markets are not pricing runaway inflation. They are pricing a high real cost of capital for a long time, which is harder on leveraged borrowers, because debts do not inflate away under it.

That cost lands on named actors. A dollar index at 103.66, its highest since April 2025, raises the price of dollar borrowing for every Asian economy whose leaders are sitting in Shenzhen this week, which is Beijing’s best argument for its own financial plumbing. A euro near $1.10, a 19-month low, squeezes the European governments borrowing for Ukraine. A 7.11 percent average mortgage rate, in the Freddie Mac survey for the week ending November 12, is the channel through which the Fed’s credibility fight reaches American housing, and Texas housing first among the fast-growing states.

Oil is the one price moving the other way, and it matters for the board. Brent crude traded at $91.62 a barrel on the morning of November 17, down 0.9 percent, and West Texas Intermediate at $84.89, down 1.0 percent, after the International Energy Agency said the world market returns to surplus this quarter as Middle East exports recover. The level is still high enough to feed headline inflation and Russian export revenue. The direction says the war premium is being sold, not bought.

December’s decision lands in a strange order. November’s inflation report arrives on December 10, the day after the vote. The Fed will hike, if it hikes, without the freshest inflation number, on a credibility argument: three straight months at 0.3 percent core is the case, and waiting for better data is the risk.

That makes December a credibility vote, not a demand-management vote. A quarter point with a hawkish set of projections does the work of a half point through guidance alone. The argument inside the committee is over how much of Musalem’s path the projections should concede.

Chapter Four

Houston

The mayor moved in three days. The county, which runs the jail and the deficit, has not moved at all.

Houston moved first, three days after the election, before Austin changed hands at all.

On November 6, Mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order narrowing when Houston police contact federal immigration authorities. Status alone is no longer a basis for a call. Contact now requires both of two things: the person is already going to jail on new criminal charges or another warrant, and there is a positive hit in the national crime database for an immigration warrant.

“Elections matter,” Whitmire said. He had consulted the incoming statewide officials and said the state’s sanctuary cities law, Senate Bill 4, is not a priority for them. The city’s own reporting counted 88 immigration-related database matches or contacts in the third quarter, and 17 people handed over in that period under the prior practice.

The order’s limits are its mechanism. It does not repeal Senate Bill 4, which bars cities from limiting cooperation with federal enforcement and remains state law. It does not touch immigration agents’ own operations in Houston. And it stops at the jailhouse door. Once a person is booked, the decision belongs to Harris County, which runs the jail, not to the police department.

Which makes the county the actor to watch. County Judge-elect Letitia Plummer, a former Houston council member, defeated Orlando Sanchez with about 61 percent of the vote and takes office in January, succeeding Lina Hidalgo. She has announced a transition and talked cooperation with Whitmire. She has announced no policy for the jail. Until she does, the county’s booking practice, the actual chokepoint in Houston’s new posture, stays exactly where the old administration left it.

Plummer’s first budget is the other January decision she cannot dodge. The county budget office put the coming year’s deficit at $189 million in August, driven by law-enforcement pay raises adopted last year, health care costs and inflation. A separate flood shortfall hangs over the projects promised in the 2018 bond: $410 million, identified in September 2025, with promised projects stopped until it is resolved. The raises are already in the base. The flood money needs revenue voters have not approved. Her mandate is fresh, and the arithmetic is not.

The Port is Houston’s physical tell, and September’s numbers carry it. Steel imports through Port Houston reached 539,993 tons in September, up 181 percent from a year earlier, while steel imports for the year to date were up only 1 percent. A one-month surge inside a flat year is a spike, not a trend, and it gives Houston’s industrial users an inventory cushion going into a year of tariff and permit fights.

The Port Commission voted on November 10 to fund the future anyway: a $569 million operating budget and a $397 million capital plan for fiscal 2027.

Houston also supplies the state transition its presiding officer in waiting. The presumptive Speaker of the Texas House is a Houstonian.

Chapter Five

Texas

The sweep was total at the top and split in the Legislature. The fights that decide the next two years are over rules, rates and the grid.

The November 3 result, stated plainly: Democrats won every statewide executive office on the ballot, ending a Republican statewide winning streak that began in 1994.

Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott, 52.8 percent to 45.6 percent. She will be the first Democratic governor since Ann Richards and the first Latina to hold the office.

James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton for the United States Senate, 55.1 percent to 43.0 percent, the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate election since 1988.

Vikki Goodwin defeated Dan Patrick for lieutenant governor, 51.7 percent to 45.6 percent. Nathan Johnson won the attorney general’s office. Democrats also took the comptroller, land and agriculture posts.

The money explains part of the Senate margin. Talarico’s campaign raised $146.3 million through mid-October. Paxton’s raised $22.3 million. More than six-to-one in cash does not win a race by itself, but it buys the saturation that turns a favourable year into a rout.

On the Railroad Commission, Houston’s Jon Rosenthal won with 52.5 percent to 45.5 percent, taking a seat on the body that regulates the state’s oil and gas industry. Republicans still hold the other two seats.

The Legislature is where the sweep stops. Democrats flipped the Texas House, 83 seats to 67, their first majority since 2003. Republicans held the Senate, 19 to 12.

That split is the governing fact of the next two years, and the fight over it started before anyone was sworn in.

The House looks settled. Senfronia Thompson of Houston, in the chamber since 1973, says she has 90 pledged supporters for Speaker, against 76 needed, including eight Republicans. Her only rival withdrew and endorsed her. She has named six former speakers, three from each party, to her transition team and promised committee chairs to both parties. Pledges are not votes, and the vote is on January 12. But a coalition bought in advance with chairs and legitimacy is the House’s governing model in miniature, and it looks stable.

The Senate is the opposite. The lieutenant governor presides over the Senate, appoints its committees, refers its bills and controls what reaches the floor. Patrick, the outgoing lieutenant governor, went on the radio on November 9 to argue that those powers rest on the Senate’s own rules, and that the Senate can change them. He said he supports Republican senators doing exactly that, moving the powers to a Republican majority leader and leaving Goodwin as presiding officer in name.

Goodwin’s counter is persuasion, conducted now, while persuasion is cheap. She has been talking to senators of both parties, laying out her plans and asking them not to strip the office. She needs Republican defections to stop a rewrite, and every senator she persuades before January is worth more than the same senator in session.

The timing is a trap built into the calendar. The Legislature convenes on January 12, 2027. The governor and lieutenant governor are not sworn in until January 19. A fast rules vote can be taken in that first week, under the old order, before Goodwin ever holds the gavel she is fighting over.

A second pressure track runs in parallel. Representative Brian Harrison has delivered 15,000 petition signatures asking Abbott to call a special session before January to limit the governor’s emergency powers under the Texas Disaster Act of 1975, the law that lets a governor issue orders with the force of law in a declared disaster and renew the declaration every 30 days. Abbott has not responded. Only the governor can call a special session, and only Abbott holds that pen until noon on January 19.

Abbott is still the most powerful person in Texas. He holds the special session call, the emergency powers being argued over, and the grid decisions described below, for ten more weeks. The election changed who proposes. It has not yet changed who disposes.

The freeze that cannot freeze

Hinojosa’s best-known pledge arrives on January 19 with her. Within an hour of taking the oath, she has said, she will declare a high-cost emergency, suspend the gas and diesel tax, and freeze electricity rates, directing the Public Utility Commission to hold residential rates until data centers and other large users pay for themselves.

The pledge runs into the structure of the Texas market. Since 2002, most of the state has bought power in a competitive retail market. In that market the retail provider sets the energy price on a household plan, not the governor and not the commission. There is no rate pen for the energy charge on a Houston bill.

What a governor and the commission can touch is the regulated wires charge, the part of the bill paid to companies like CenterPoint in Houston, whose increases the commission approves. The commission cannot be restaffed on day one either. Its members are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Senate, and confirmation, when her appointments come, runs through the Republican Senate described above.

The disaster route is untested. Whether high cost counts as a disaster under the 1975 act, and whether a declaration can write a price the market structure does not allow, would be decided by courts, not by the order. The Harrison petition shows the other side already working to narrow those same emergency powers before she can use them.

The pledge is best read as an opening bid in a legislative negotiation. Its real target is the session’s central trade: what large power users pay, and who gets cut first when power runs short.

The grid fight underneath

ERCOT’s chief executive, Pablo Vegas, made his ask in Houston on November 11, at a BloombergNEF summit. He wants the Legislature to let the grid operator order data centers and other large loads to cut power at the first sign of scarcity, before an emergency is declared, so the burden stays off households and small businesses.

Current law is later and weaker. Senate Bill 6, passed in 2025, lets ERCOT order the largest users, those at 75 megawatts and above with backup power, to cut or switch to backup late in an emergency, on a day’s notice through a separate programme still being built. ERCOT has never ordered a data center to curtail under it. The cuts taken last winter were voluntary, in the low single-digit gigawatts by Vegas’s own account.

Vegas is asking for authority he partly holds and has never used, moved earlier in the sequence. That does not make the ask hollow. Timing is the substance. A cut ordered at the first warning is a planning input a data center can price. A cut ordered inside an emergency is a loss.

The queue behind the fight is mostly paper, and the chart above is the deflation. ERCOT’s Batch Zero study kept 362 projects totalling 191.8 gigawatts for study and excluded another 302.2 gigawatts of requests. Of the kept requests, 66.4 gigawatts counts as base load. Requests are free options. Developers file them to hold a place, not to commit capital.

The concrete near-term fact is small: 17 loads totalling about 6.6 gigawatts have cleared everything except permission to switch on, and are waiting on reports due to the Public Utility Commission by December 10.

Those reports are the hinge of the whole Texas energy story. Abbott paused new large-load energising in August pending an ERCOT audit. The pause in force today is the outgoing Republican’s, not the incoming Democrat’s. What Hinojosa inherits on January 19 is Abbott’s audit, Abbott’s appointees at the commission, and a December 10 report that will frame the session’s argument before she writes a word of it.

The market has already priced the uncertainty. Vistra, the state’s largest power generator, fell about 14 percent on November 4. That is policy risk being priced, not megawatts being cancelled. Projects with interconnection and permits already secured are worth more under every scenario, because scarcity raises the value of what is already allowed to run.

The cost side of the buildout is the political fuel. One recent modelling study of 371 announced Texas data center projects found they could add about 1.64 cents per kilowatt-hour to household costs in peak season, roughly two thirds of it through higher wholesale prices and a third through transmission, with about $32.4 billion of transmission reinforcement required. It is a modelled estimate, not a bill. It is still the number the session will argue about, because it converts an abstract queue into a line on a household statement.

Houston sits on both sides of this. It sells the energy and hosts the load. Cheap natural gas, with winter Henry Hub forecast near $2.87, protects the margins of the generators and LNG exporters along the Ship Channel, while expensive capital, at a 5 percent Treasury yield, raises the hurdle for every new project that needs financing. The winners of a high-rate, tight-grid Texas are the incumbents: existing generation, contracted exports, secured interconnections. The losers are new entrants who must borrow at the new curve to join a queue that is mostly paper.

Chapter Six

Two Rival Reads

Was this week the pricing or the event? Two coherent answers, and the tests that separate them.

Read one: the pricing is the event. Nothing binding happened this week, and the signals were designed that way. A summit with no text, a strike on a repairable bridge, a futures print, a campaign pledge, a curtailment request to a legislature that does not sit until January. Each actor spent something cheap and reversible to improve the price of a later negotiation. On this read, the board in January looks much like the board today, with better-rehearsed positions.

Read two: the formats are the event. Power moved this week in the only place it ever moves first, which is who sits where. A three-president format that did not exist now exists, and formats outlive meetings. Europe sat inside the Ukraine talks in full for the first time, and a seat once taken is hard to take back. The Texas Senate’s rules fight and ERCOT’s curtailment ask are both contests over procedure that will decide substance for years. On this read, Thursday in Shenzhen, the Berlin meeting, the rules vote in January and the December 10 grid reports are not preludes. They are the decisions, arriving in procedural dress.

What decides between them is observable, and each test is separate.

If Shenzhen produces a signed text that mentions Ukraine or nuclear limits, read two gains and read one is in trouble.

If rail traffic over the Kerch Bridge is still halted a week from now, with the rail span confirmed down, the strike was substance, not signal.

If the European Council unlocks Ukraine’s 2027 money over the holdouts’ objections, Europe’s seat was bought and paid for.

If the Texas Senate rewrites its rules in the week of January 12, procedure was the power all along.

If all four come back empty, read one stands: a week of pricing, settled nowhere.

Chapter Seven

Scenarios

Three ways the board moves from here, each with the evidence that would confirm it and the evidence that would kill it.

The tables harden. Shenzhen issues a joint statement with a nuclear dialogue channel and named follow-ups, Moscow accepts the Berlin format for a next round, and the European Council unlocks the 2027 money. Confirm it with documents and dates, not communiques about dialogue. Kill it if Thursday ends with three separate national readouts and no shared text.

The pricing unwinds. The inflation data softens, the December hike shrinks to an insurance move, Shenzhen produces photographs only, the bridge carries rail traffic as normal, and Abbott lifts or narrows his own grid pause before leaving. Confirm it in the December 9 vote split and the December 10 ERCOT reports. Kill it if the October meeting minutes show the hawkish bloc already had the votes before the inflation print.

Escalation reprices everything. A follow-on strike closes the Kerch rail span, tanker traffic through Hormuz is hit again, Brent pushes back toward its October highs, and the half-point tail in Fed pricing fattens into the meeting. Confirm it in freight and war-risk insurance pricing and in the half-point share of futures pricing, not in drone tallies. Kill it if oil keeps sliding on the IEA surplus and the half-point share stays in single digits.

Chapter Eight

Watchlist

Five developments that would change the analysis.

The October FOMC minutes. How broad the hawkish bloc was before the inflation print decides whether December is about one hike or several.

Shenzhen, November 19, and the Berlin meeting. Two rooms, each missing the party the other one needs. A shared Shenzhen text, or Moscow accepting Europeans in the next Ukraine round, would be the week’s first settled fact.

The European Council’s next summit. It decides whether Ukraine’s 2027 money beyond the existing loan is a commitment or an argument, and whether Merz’s budget linkage breaks the holdouts or breaks the budget.

December 9 and December 10. The Fed votes on the 9th. November inflation and the ERCOT and Public Utility Commission reports arrive on the 10th. Two of the board’s open questions price within 24 hours of each other.

The Texas Senate rules vote, week of January 12. It decides whether the lieutenant governor governs the Senate or merely presides over it, and it happens before the new officeholders are sworn in, which is the point.
